title: The backport does not apply cleanly
summary: The release branch has drifted, so the fix will not apply as written. Resolve the conflict, continue, and learn the flags for picking several commits and for stopping before the commit.
mental_model: Cherry-pick is a sequencer, like rebase: it applies commits one at a time and pauses on failure with a conflicted index. `--continue` resumes, `--abort` unwinds everything, `--skip` drops the current one.

commit.message: Add logging on the release branch

steps.title: See why it will not apply cleanly
steps.why: Both branches edited the same function for different reasons. The fix's diff expects the release branch's version of those lines, and it is not there.

steps.title: Attempt the backport
steps.why: Cherry-pick stops with a conflicted index, exactly like a merge. Read the message: it names the commit it was applying, which matters when you are picking several.
commands: sh -c 'git cherry-pick -x $(git log -1 --format=%H --grep="Validate request body" main)'

verify.label: the cherry-pick paused on a conflict

steps.title: Look at the sequencer state
steps.why: `.git/sequencer` holds the in-progress operation, and `CHERRY_PICK_HEAD` names the commit being applied. This is how git knows what `--continue` should finish.
steps.expect: The commit you are backporting, by name.

steps.title: Prove abort is available
steps.why: `--abort` restores the branch and working tree completely. Every sequencer operation in git has this exit, and knowing it is there makes the conflict much less stressful.
steps.expect: Back to the release branch's own version, tree clean.

verify.label: the abort left a clean tree

steps.title: Retry and resolve properly
steps.why: Keep the release branch's logging AND add the validation. A backport is a code change, not a mechanical patch application — the result should be right for this branch, not identical to main.

actions.run: sh -c 'git cherry-pick -x $(git log -1 --format=%H --grep="Validate request body" main)'

steps.expect: Nothing conflicted, the resolution staged, the pick still in progress.

steps.title: Continue — never commit
steps.why: `--continue` finishes the pick using the original message plus the `-x` provenance line. Running `git commit` here would work but would lose that message and leave the sequencer running.

verify.label: the provenance survived the conflict resolution
both the branch's logging and the backported validation are present

steps.title: Pick without committing — and note what changes
steps.why: `-n` applies the change and stages it without making a commit, so a series can land as one squashed backport. It conflicts here too, and this time there is no `--continue` to run: with `-n` there is no sequencer, so you resolve, stage and commit yourself.
steps.expect: Four commits on the release branch, and no sequencer state to clean up.

verify.label: the second backport landed as your own commit
verify.hint: git cherry-pick -n <sha>, resolve, then commit yourself

verify.label: both backports applied, and the branch's own logging survived
verify.hint: resolve the conflict keeping both sides, then --continue

verify.label: provenance is recorded for the first backport
the release branch has its own commit for each backport

pitfalls: Use `git cherry-pick --continue`, not `git commit`. Committing by hand leaves the sequencer half-finished and drops the -x line.
`--skip` abandons the commit being applied. On a multi-commit pick it is easy to skip something you needed.
A conflict-free cherry-pick is not proof of correctness. A fix that assumes code the release branch does not have can apply cleanly and still be wrong.
`git cherry-pick A..B` picks a range; note it excludes A itself, exactly like log ranges.
With `-n` there is no sequencer state, so `--continue` does not apply. Resolve, `git add`, and commit yourself.
